variants.name: Typed mapping function over DTO interfaces
variants.idiom_name: typed mapping function between declared DTO interfaces (zod at untrusted seams)
variants.implementation_notes: The translator is a typed function between two declared interfaces (function toCanonical(w: LegacyOrderDto): OrderDto), with a discriminated union plus switch when several wire versions share a channel; the mapping is ordinary object construction, and the value of the pattern is the explicit, separately reviewed DTO pair. Because interfaces are erased at runtime, a schema library takes over validation at untrusted seams: a zod object schema with .transform(...) validates and translates in one pass and z.infer keeps the static type in sync (zod.dev). Keep DTOs in their own module so the foreign shape never leaks inward, and use codegen (protobuf.js) when the wire contract is IDL-owned.
pitfalls: Types are erased, so an unvalidated cast (wire as LegacyOrderDto) is exactly where malformed messages enter the system; validate the payload before the mapping runs.
noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off by default, so w['qty'] type-checks as number although it is undefined at runtime for an absent field.
JSON.parse turns 64-bit ids and Dates into lossy numbers/strings, and strict TS types keep claiming the original type; translate ids as strings and dates explicitly.

variants.name: zod schema with .transform at the seam
variants.implementation_notes: Declare one schema per side of the seam and let the schema both validate and translate: z.object({ order_id: z.string(), qty: z.number().int().positive() }).transform(({ order_id, qty }) => ({ id: order_id, quantity: qty })) returns the canonical shape from .parse/safeParse, and z.infer<typeof schema> supplies the static type so the mapping cannot drift from the runtime shape (zod.dev). Choose it when the payload is untrusted or the contract is only documented, and accept the dependency plus a runtime parse per message.
pitfalls: safeParse returns a result object instead of throwing: ignoring result.success silently gives the next stage `undefined` where a canonical message was expected.

Overloaded .transform chains make the inferred target type surprising, and transforms are not applied in the reverse direction - a schema-first translator still needs an explicit encoder for the outbound message.
Zod 3 parse costs are real on hot paths; prefer compile-time mappers (or precompiled validators) for high-volume seams and keep the schema at the trust boundary only.
